POV: you're in tech in 2026 and you get to choose one of four life paths.

A — Take the badge.
Join the biggest tech employer in your country, the one with its logo on a tower. Post a mirror selfie with your badge every Monday, develop strong opinions about the free canteen, and enjoy the quiet status of working somewhere your relatives have actually heard of. You will date someone from a neighbouring team and get the corporate mortgage rate that nobody outside the company can get. And you will be fine. Genuinely, comfortably fine, for eleven years.

B — Go fully remote.
Work for a company registered in Dubai, from a co-living in Bali, for a client whose name you have never been told. Get paid in USDT under compliance conditions best described as fifty-fifty. Earn two to three times your local market. Have a CV with five years of experience and the word NDA where the employers should be. Tell everyone you're fully remote, which is completely true: you are fully, permanently, at home. You do go outside. For groceries. Not often.

C — Get the real thing.
Join actual Big Tech, Google or Amazon, clear the visa, relocate, and enjoy a quiet sense of superiority over everyone in A and B. Then hand most of your salary to a tax authority you cannot vote for, spend what's left on the car, and have it broken into in month two, in a neighbourhood the listing described as vibrant. Your closest friend within four thousand kilometres is your manager.

D — Build.
Launch an infinite series of AI-for-AI B2C-B2B-B2B2C-B2B2B SaaS startups with a combined revenue of $100. Live on your mum's money. Post photos from conferences. Have a small nervous breakdown every time OpenAI or Anthropic ships anything. Eventually arrive at A, B or C anyway.

Asking for a friend. The friend is me, and the friend is standing at this fork right now with an unreasonable number of tabs open.

Aiming for C. Would happily take a grown-up version of B, the kind with a real contract and a company name I'm allowed to say out loud. Actively avoiding D.

Senior / Principal Product Manager. AI and agentic products, platform, MedTech. Ready to relocate.

If you're hiring for one of those, my profile is one click up and to the left.

The financial AI workbench has arrived as a category — OpenAI with hosted datasets and entitlement connections, LSEG putting agents inside Workspace, FactSet embedding a specialist partner, S&P Global running both routes at once. What's being sold is assembly: model, licensed evidence, connectors, templates, controls, audit logs under one contract.
What is not being sold is ownership of the inputs. And that boundary decides who can actually use it.
A bank producing an internal valuation and a consultancy publishing a market database may ask the model identical questions and sit in completely different licensing positions. Bundled terms typically permit internal research while prohibiting model training, bulk export, database reconstruction and CRM population. The closer your output gets to the data vendor's own product, the less a standard bundle covers you.
The point almost nobody prices: released hours are not saved money. Illustratively, one hour per person per month across a 100-person team at €75 fully loaded is €90,000 a year of capacity. If analysts simply finish earlier and headcount is unchanged, the accounting saving is zero. Value appears only where capacity converts into mandates won, coverage extended, outsourcing cut or hiring avoided — and those chains run differently for a bank, a wealth manager and an in-house corporate finance team.

Somewhere in your company there is a compliance officer whose job just got automated. Not by AI. By 40 lines of Solidity.

Stablecoins moved $27.6 trillion last year. More than Visa and Mastercard combined. Most of that plumbing is not written by banks. It is written by people like me, in a text editor, on a Tuesday.

I built a collateralized stablecoin protocol this year. Eight modules. Oracle with fallback feeds, Dutch auction liquidations, repeg, a rate limiter on mint and burn.

Somewhere around module five I noticed something I did not like. I was not writing finance anymore. I was writing policy. Nobody asked me to.

The rate limiter is the issuer brake a supervisor demands once daily flows get serious. The reserve checks are MiCA and the GENIUS Act asking for 1 to 1, verifiable, right now. The oracle fallback exists because someone, at some point, had to explain a depeg to a board.

All of that used to live in a PDF. Now it is an invariant test. Passes or fails. No meeting, no memo, no second opinion.

Here is the uncomfortable part. The person who wrote that PDF never saw my code. And I never read their PDF. We wrote the same rule twice, in two languages, and only one of them runs.

Circle, Bridge, Paxos are hiring for exactly this seat. Go read their smart contract openings. Regulatory literacy sits next to Foundry in the same line. I have, more than once, and it changed what I build.

So one honest question, whichever floor you sit on.

Is the rule you are responsible for written in something that executes? Or in something that gets ignored?

Sales needs an answer from Product.

 Finance needs numbers from Operations.
 Operations needs the founder to clarify priority.
So the founder becomes the integration layer.
Everything works.
Until it doesn’t.
The symptoms usually look like:
→ decisions waiting for one person
 → the same questions being answered repeatedly
 → updates living across Slack, email and meetings
 → teams unsure who actually owns the next step
 → the founder carrying context that should live in the system
At that point, the problem is not simply “we need better project management.”
It is:
How do we remove unnecessary dependence on the founder without losing judgment?
That is where I think good Operations / Chief of Staff work becomes valuable.
The job is to turn founder-held context into:
Clear ownership
 Decision rules
 Escalation thresholds
 Reliable handoffs
 Shared operating data
 Automation where repetition adds no value
And increasingly, AI can help with part of that layer:
Context gathering → exception detection → summaries → recommendations → routing
But the operating logic still matters more than the model.

Sometimes the HealthTech roadmap isn't the problem.

The team available to deliver it is.
A HealthTech company can have a clear roadmap:
A new patient app.
An EHR integration.
AI capabilities.
Platform modernization.
Better analytics.
A major customer implementation.
And still struggle to deliver on time.
Not because the engineering team isn't capable.
Because they're already at capacity.
Then hiring starts.
Java developers.
.NET engineers.
Data engineers.
Cloud specialists.
QA automation.
AI/ML talent.
And suddenly, a product deadline has also become a recruitment deadline.
This is something I think HealthTech companies need to plan for earlier.
Because finding a developer isn't necessarily difficult.
Finding someone with the right technical depth, healthcare context and availability — at the moment the roadmap needs them — is a very different challenge.
Sometimes permanent hiring is the right answer.
Sometimes you need contract capacity for 6 months.
Sometimes you need a niche specialist for one critical project.
The hiring model can change.
But the objective shouldn't:
Don't let an open position become a product bottleneck.
Over the next few weeks, I'll be sharing more about the technology hiring challenges I see across HealthTech and Healthcare IT — and how companies can build engineering capacity without compromising on talent quality.
